a: the tenth day of the fifth month
t: The fifth month, or no month named?
p: The Hebrew says "the fifth month, the tenth day"; Codex Vaticanus says only "the fifteenth of the month", with no month number.

readings.en: in the fifth, on the tenth of the month
readings.plain: the tenth day of the fifth month

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), Codex Vaticanus in Swete's text
readings.en: on the fifteenth of the month
readings.plain: the fifteenth day of the month

why: The Hebrew has Ezekiel's usual way of giving a day, "on the tenth of the month" (24:1; 40:1), and it names the month. The Greek in Codex Vaticanus has a different day (fifteen, not ten) and no month number. No Qumran scroll preserves this verse. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.
b: Ezekiel's other dates in this part, 24:1 and 40:1, are also the tenth day. A scribe or translator may have been influenced by a nearby date or by a different Hebrew number, and the Greek may have dropped the month. The change moves the date by five days, and without the month it also loses the fifth month. The meaning is not affected. The page of the chapter says which Greek witnesses were read.

a: bring you into the covenant's bond
t: Bond of the covenant, or by number?
p: The Hebrew has a rare word "bond"; the Greek has "by number".

readings.en: and I will bring you into the bond of the covenant
readings.plain: bring you into the covenant's bond

readings.en: and I will bring you in by number
readings.plain: bring you in by number

why: The Hebrew word masoret is found only here and is related to the verb for "bind" (asar). The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew, which makes good sense with the "covenant" of the rest of the verse. No Qumran scroll preserves this verse.
b: The Greek "by number" would fit a counting of the flock "under the rod" (the first half of the verse), and may reflect a different Hebrew word (a word for "number", mispar, has been suggested). The choice is discussed in the commentaries; the Hebrew word has also been tied to the later word for "tradition" (masorah), which is a later use.

a: turn your face toward the south
p: The Hebrew has three words for the south; the Greek turns two of them into place names.

readings.en: toward the south... the south... the Negev
readings.plain: turn your face toward the south

readings.en: toward Teman... toward Dagon... the Negev
readings.plain: turn your face toward Teman

why: The Hebrew uses ordinary words for "south" (teimanah, darom) and the region name Negev. The Greek writes Thaiman and Dagon as names, which may come from reading the words as place names. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew, since the point is the direction.
b: In the Greek, the three names are Teman, Dagon and the forest of the Nageb. Teman is also the name of an Edomite region (Amos 1:12), so some ancient readers may have heard an oracle against Edom. No Qumran scroll preserves the verse.

a: cut the righteous and the wicked off from you
t: The righteous and the wicked, or the lawless?
p: The Hebrew has "the righteous and the wicked"; Codex Vaticanus has "the unrighteous and the lawless". This goes with the next entry.

readings.en: the righteous and the wicked
readings.plain: cut the righteous and the wicked off from you

readings.en: the unrighteous and the lawless
readings.plain: cut the unrighteous and the lawless off from you

why: The Hebrew is the harder reading, since it sets the sword against chapter 18. The Greek removes the difficulty, which is a reason to suspect the Greek of smoothing. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew, since the Greek's wording is as likely to be a softening as the sign of a different Hebrew text.
b: Rashi on this verse (Hebrew 21:8, as translated on Sefaria) reads "the righteous and the wicked" as "the moist and the dry", the green and dry trees of 20:47, which shows that Jewish readers felt the problem and answered it inside the Hebrew. The Talmud's discussion of the righteous who die with the wicked (Bavli Shabbat 55a–b) is built on Ezekiel 9:4–6, not on this verse. No Qumran scroll preserves this verse. The Greek repeats its reading in 21:4.

a: cut the righteous and the wicked off from you
t: The righteous and the wicked, or the lawless?
p: The same difference as in 21:3. This goes with the previous entry.

readings.en: the righteous and the wicked
readings.plain: cut the righteous and the wicked off from you

readings.en: the unrighteous and the lawless
readings.plain: cut the unrighteous and the lawless off from you

why: As in 21:3: the Hebrew is the harder reading, and the Greek gives the easier. No Qumran scroll preserves the verse.

a: A ruin, a ruin, a ruin: that is what I will make it. And this too will not remain
p: The Hebrew has "ruin" three times and "this too will not remain"; Codex Vaticanus has "injustice" three times, "woe to her" and "such it will be".

readings.orig: עַוָּה עַוָּה עַוָּה אֲשִׂימֶנָּה גַּם־זֹאת לֹא הָיָה עַד־בֹּא אֲשֶׁר־לוֹ הַמִּשְׁפָּט וּנְתַתִּיו
readings.en: a ruin, a ruin, a ruin I will make it; this too will not be, until he comes whose is the right, and I will give it to him
readings.plain: A ruin, a ruin, a ruin: that is what I will make it. And this too will not remain

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), Codex Vaticanus in Swete's text
readings.orig: ἀδικίαν ἀδικίαν ἀδικίαν θήσομαι αὐτήν, οὐαὶ αὐτῇ· τοιαύτη ἔσται ἕως οὗ ἔλθῃ ᾧ καθήκει, καὶ παραδώσω αὐτῷ
readings.en: injustice, injustice, injustice I will make it, woe to her; such it will be until he comes for whom it is fitting, and I will hand it over to him
readings.plain: Injustice, injustice, injustice: that is what I will make it. Woe to her! It will be like this until he comes for whom it is fitting, and I will hand it over to him.

why: The Greek renders the Hebrew rare word for "ruin" with the common word for "injustice", adds "woe to her", and says "such it will be" where the Hebrew says "this too will not be". The last clause, "until he comes for whom it is fitting", matches the Hebrew in sense. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew, which is the harder text. No Qumran scroll preserves this verse.
b: The Greek "until he comes for whom it is fitting" is as open as the Hebrew "whose right it is": it fits a historical ruler and a messianic reader equally, and it does not name God. See the notes on the verse.

a: You will be profaned in yourself
t: Profaned, or I will take possession?
p: The Hebrew can mean "be profaned" or "take possession"; the Greek read it as "take possession".

readings.en: and you will be profaned in yourself (from chalal)
readings.plain: You will be profaned in yourself

readings.en: and I will take possession in you (from nachal)
readings.plain: I will take possession in you

why: The consonants allow both. The Plain English Translation takes the Hebrew as it is vocalized, "you will be profaned", which fits the chapter's use of the word (22:8, 26) and the "scattering" of 22:15. No Qumran scroll preserves the verse.
b: The Greek reads the same consonants from nachal, which gives a sentence about God taking possession. The choice is discussed in the commentaries. The Greek alone has the second reading.

p: The Hebrew has "her prophets" here; Codex Vaticanus has "leaders".

readings.en: her prophets
readings.plain: Her prophets

readings.en: the leaders (as if nesi'eha)
readings.plain: Her leaders

why: The Hebrew text has prophets, and the list in 22:25–29 names prophets twice (22:25, 28). Prophets and leaders look alike in Hebrew letters (nevi'eha and nesi'eha), so a copy may have gone either way. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew. No Qumran scroll preserves the verse.
b: Zephaniah 3:3–4 has officials, judges, prophets and priests in that order. Here 22:25 and 22:27 would both be officials if the Greek were followed, and the prophets would be named only once (22:28).

a: someone to build up a wall and take a stand in the gap in front of me for the land's sake
t: Wall and gap, or a man who lives rightly?
p: Codex Vaticanus has no wall and no gap: the LORD looks for a man who lives rightly.

readings.orig: גֹּדֵר־גָּדֵר וְעֹמֵד בַּפֶּרֶץ לְפָנַי בְּעַד הָאָרֶץ
readings.en: one who builds a wall and stands in the breach before me for the land
readings.plain: someone to build up a wall and take a stand in the gap in front of me for the land's sake

readings.orig: ἄνδρα ἀναστρεφόμενον ὀρθῶς καὶ ἑστῶτα πρὸ προσώπου μου ὁλοσχερῶς ἐν καιρῷ τῆς γῆς
readings.en: a man living rightly and standing before me completely in the time of the land
readings.plain: a man who lived rightly, someone to stand before me completely in the time of the land's trouble

why: The Hebrew picture of a wall and a gap is vivid and fits Ezekiel 13:5. The Greek has a plainer line, which a translator may have made when the image of a wall was hard. No Qumran scroll preserves the verse.
b: Some scholars think the Greek translator simplified. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew, whose image is also known elsewhere (Psalm 106:23).

t: Tearing the breasts, or ending her feasts?
p: The Hebrew has her tearing her breasts; Codex Vaticanus has the LORD turning away her feasts.

readings.en: and you will tear your breasts
readings.plain: and rip at your breasts

readings.orig: τὰς ἑορτὰς καὶ τὰς νεομηνίας αὐτῆς ἀποστρέψω
readings.en: I will turn away her feasts and her new moons
readings.plain: and I will turn her feasts and her new moons away

why: The Hebrew is the fuller and the harder text. The Greek has a different clause, with "feasts and new moons", a phrase known from 45:17 and Hosea 2:11. No Qumran scroll preserves the verse.
b: The Greek may reflect a different Hebrew (or a freer rendering of a hard line, since "gnaw its pieces" is also missing from the Greek).

t: Sabeans, drunkards, or men of the desert?
p: The written Hebrew says "drunkards", the reading tradition says "Sabeans", and the Greek says neither.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Qere (the reading tradition), printed in the Leningrad Codex
readings.en: Sabeans
readings.plain: Sabeans from the wilderness

readings.en: drunkards
readings.plain: drunkards from the wilderness

readings.en: men coming from the wilderness
readings.plain: men from the wilderness

why: The Qere names a people from Sheba who trade through the desert (Job 1:15; Joel 3:8). The Ketiv, "drunkards", is also possible beside "a carefree crowd". The Plain English Translation follows the Qere, which is the reading of the Leningrad Codex's margin. No Qumran scroll preserves the verse (4Q73 preserves parts of 23:14, 15, 17, 18 and 23:44–47 only).
b: The Ketiv and Qere were kept side by side by the scribes. The Greek omits the word.

a: A man would come to her
p: The Masoretic Text has "he went in"; a Qumran scroll and the Greek have the plural.

readings.en: and he went in to her
readings.plain: A man would come to her

readings.w: 4QEzek-a (4Q73, as transcribed by Abegg, Bowley and Cook); Greek (Swete's text)
readings.en: and they went in to her
readings.plain: They would come to her

why: The singular is a general statement ("as a man goes in to a prostitute") and suits the clause that follows. The plural is possible: the Qumran letters can be read "they went in", while the Masoretic letters are singular. The transcription marks the difference as one of waw and yod, so it is a candidate and not a settled variant. The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic Text.
b: The Greek verb is plural and imperfect ("they were going in"). 4QEzek-a (4Q73) also preserves parts of 23:14, 15, 17, 18 and 23:45–47. The Plain English Translation does not rest on a scroll for this verse.

a: They will judge you by your ways and by your deeds
t: They judge you, or I judge you?
p: The Hebrew has "they will judge you"; the Greek has "I will judge you", and says it twice.

readings.en: they will judge you
readings.plain: They will judge you by your ways and by your deeds

readings.en: I will judge you
readings.plain: I will judge you by your ways and by your deeds

why: The Hebrew third-person plural may be impersonal ("you will be judged") or may mean the Babylonians, as in 23:24 ("they will judge you by their own judgments"). The Greek puts it in the LORD's own mouth and adds a doublet. 4QEzek-c (4Q75) preserves only 24:2–3, so no scroll bears on this verse.
b: The Greek also repeats the sentence in a longer form. The Plain English Translation does not rest on the Greek here.
